title: Socio-Economic Development and Empowerment of Disadvantaged Groups
summary: ## Socio-economic development

Development means a state in which things are improving. In the socio-economic sense it means improving people's lifestyles through better education, incomes, skills and employment. It is measured with indicators such as GDP, life expectancy, literacy and levels of employment.

Social development transforms social institutions so that society can fulfil its aspirations — more progressive attitudes, better processes and technology. Economic development is the growth of economic wealth for people's well-being; economic growth means a rise in national income, GDP or per capita income, while economic development is wider — improving the economic, political and social well-being of people.

GDP is the total value of all final goods and services produced within a country in a year. National income is the total income of a nation's people in a year. Per capita income = national income ÷ population. Limits: GDP ignores leisure, environment, freedom, social justice and gender equality; per capita income does not show how equally income is shared. So the idea of human development came in.
## Human development and HDI

Human development enlarges people's choices and well-being in all aspects of life — income is only one part; it puts people at the centre of development. The concept was introduced by Dr. Mahbub ul Haq (Pakistani economist); Amartya Sen defined it as development that increases freedoms. The Human Development Index (HDI) was developed in 1990 and is used by the UNDP in its annual Human Development Report.

HDI has three indices: (1) a long and healthy life — life expectancy at birth; (2) knowledge and education — adult literacy rate and gross enrolment ratio; (3) a decent standard of living — GDP per capita in PPP US dollars. India ranked 128 of 177 countries in 2007–08 (medium category). Topography, for example, is not an HDI indicator.
## Sustainable development

'Development that meets the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs.' It covers economic, social, individual and environmental development and the needs of all sections including disadvantaged groups.
## Development in India

Since 1990 India has been one of the fastest-growing economies (fourth largest by GDP in PPP terms), with rising life expectancy, literacy and food security. But 27.5% lived below the poverty line in 2004–05, about 80% lived on less than US$2 a day, and 40% of children under three were underweight — development and under-development co-exist. Purchasing Power Parity (PPP) compares living standards by what currencies can actually buy.
## Regional imbalances

Natural differences (plains vs. hills, fertile vs. poor soil) are diversity; human-made inequalities in income, agriculture, industry, transport, literacy and health are disparities. Per capita income: national average Rs 25,716 (2005–06); the poorest States were Bihar, UP, MP, Orissa, Rajasthan, Jharkhand and Chhattisgarh. Poverty: rural Orissa 43%, rural Bihar 40% vs. rural Punjab 2.4%. Agriculture: Punjab, Haryana, UP ahead. Literacy (2001): Kerala 90.92%, Bihar 47.53% (India 65.38%). Road length: Kerala highest, J&K lowest.

Causes of regional disparities: (1) historical — colonial neglect of areas not useful commercially (tribal Central and North-East India); (2) geographical — deserts and hilly terrain; (3) unequal distribution and use of natural resources (Bihar, Jharkhand, Orissa have minerals but stay poor); (4) remoteness from national markets; (5) lack of infrastructure — roads, power, transport; (6) poor governance and law-and-order problems.
## Disadvantaged groups
Groups discriminated socially and economically and unable to share fully in development: Scheduled Castes (16.23% in 2001), Scheduled Tribes (8.2%), OBCs, minorities and women.

Empowerment of SCs and STs — a three-pronged strategy: (a) Social empowerment through education — no tuition fee, free books, mid-day meals, scholarships (pre-matric, post-matric, Rajiv Gandhi National Fellowship), Kasturba Gandhi Balika Vidyalaya, Navodaya Vidyalaya, coaching and hostels. (b) Economic empowerment — NSFDC, NSKFDC (safai karamcharis), NSTFDC, SC/ST Development Corporations and TRIFED (marketing of minor forest produce). (c) Social justice — Protection of Civil Rights Act 1955, SC/ST (Prevention of Atrocities) Act 1989, Forest Rights Act 2006.

Women's empowerment: gender equality is in the Preamble, Fundamental Rights, Duties and Directive Principles, and the State may make special provisions for women. Economic — poverty programmes for women, training in agriculture, labour laws and social security, crèches. Social — equal education, health and nutrition, ending violence. Political — right to vote and contest; the 73rd and 74th Amendments (1993) reserved 33.3% of local-body seats for women; a Bill for reservation in Lok Sabha and Assemblies was then under consideration (passed in 2023).
## Education for all

Jomtien (Thailand) 1990 conference under UNESCO: Education for All by 2000; Delhi meeting of nine populous countries in 1992. National Policy on Education 1986: free and compulsory education up to 14; the 86th Amendment (2002) made it a Fundamental Right for 6–14-year-olds; the RTE Act 2009. Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan (2001) — enrol all 6–14-year-olds, bridge gender and social gaps, universal retention, quality education. Mid-day Meal Scheme — nutrition for classes I–V and regular attendance. Steps to reduce drop-out: parental awareness, community and PRI involvement, free books and uniforms, better schooling, mid-day meals.

National Literacy Mission (1988): functional literacy for adults aged 15–35 through the Total Literacy Campaign, Post Literacy Programme, Continuing Education Programme and Jan Shikshan Sansthans; literacy rose from 52.21% (1991) to 65.37% (2001); now an integrated approach.
## Health for all

India launched the world's first Family Planning Programme (1951). 'Health for All by 2000' was declared at Alma Ata (1978). Since health facilities are concentrated in cities, the National Rural Health Mission (NRHM) was started to provide health care in rural areas, along with Janani Suraksha Yojana, Balika Samridhi Yojana and Kishori Shakti Yojana; the National Urban Health Mission followed. Achievements: death rate 27.4 → 8.5 per thousand, infant mortality 134 → 71, life expectancy 32 → 65 years (1947–2001).

vsa: Why do GDP and per capita income not effectively measure the quality of people's life?

GDP ignores leisure, environmental quality, freedom, social justice and gender equality. Per capita income is only an average and does not show inequality of income, so it cannot tell whether the benefits of development reach the poor and disadvantaged.
Differentiate between diversity and disparity with examples.

Diversity is a natural difference between regions — e.g. the fertile Ganga plain versus hilly, forested North-East. Disparity is a human-made inequality in income, industry, literacy, health or roads — e.g. Kerala's 90.92% literacy versus Bihar's 47.53% (2001).
Mention any two indicators of socio-economic development.
Any two: per capita income / GDP; literacy rate; life expectancy; level of employment; infant mortality; access to health care.
What is sustainable development? Give one example.

Development that meets the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs. Example: using solar or wind energy and rainwater harvesting instead of over-using coal and groundwater.
Why are the tribal areas of central India underdeveloped?

They were neglected under colonial rule because they had little commercial value, have hilly forested terrain and poor infrastructure, few industries, and low economic and human development of local people.
sa: Explain any three causes of regional disparities in India.

(1) Historical — areas not useful to the British, like tribal Central and North-East India, were neglected. (2) Geographical — deserts of Rajasthan and hilly terrain of the North-East restrict development; remoteness from national markets. (3) Lack of infrastructure and poor governance — States without roads, power and law and order cannot attract investment or use funds well.
Describe the three-pronged strategy adopted for the empowerment of Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes.

(1) Social empowerment — education with free books, no fees, mid-day meals, scholarships, hostels, coaching, Kasturba Gandhi Balika Vidyalaya. (2) Economic empowerment — loans and support from NSFDC, NSKFDC, NSTFDC, SC/ST Development Corporations and marketing help from TRIFED. (3) Social justice — protective laws such as the Protection of Civil Rights Act 1955, Prevention of Atrocities Act 1989 and Forest Rights Act 2006.
Explain any three measures taken by the government for the economic and social empowerment of women.

(1) Poverty eradication and training programmes addressed to women's needs, especially in agriculture. (2) Labour laws, social security and support services such as crèches to help women work in industry. (3) Equal access to education, health and nutrition and elimination of violence against women; politically, one-third reservation in local bodies.

or: What is the role of the National Rural Health Mission? Mention any two other health programmes for women and children.

Medical facilities are concentrated in cities, so NRHM was launched to provide accessible, affordable health care in rural areas, reducing the rural–urban gap. Other programmes: Janani Suraksha Yojana, Balika Samridhi Yojana, Kishori Shakti Yojana (any two).

sa: Describe any three measures adopted to reduce drop-out rates and improve achievement in schools.

(1) Creating parental awareness and mobilising the community and Panchayati Raj Institutions. (2) Economic incentives — free education, free books and uniforms, scholarships. (3) Mid-day Meal Scheme and improvement in the content and process of schooling.
What are the goals of Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan?

(1) Enrolment of all children of 6–14 years in school or alternative centres. (2) Bridging gender and social category gaps at the primary and elementary levels. (3) Universal retention and elementary education of satisfactory quality with emphasis on education for life.
How is human development different from economic development?

(1) Economic development focuses mainly on income and wealth; human development enlarges all choices of people — health, education, freedom, culture. (2) Human development puts people at the centre; income is only one component. (3) It cares about quality and distribution of growth, measured by HDI (life expectancy, education, standard of living) rather than GDP alone.
la: What is the Human Development Index? Explain its three indices and dimensions, and state India's position.

HDI, developed in 1990 by economists including Mahbub ul Haq and Amartya Sen, is used by UNDP in its annual Human Development Report to measure a country's level of development. (1) A long and healthy life — life expectancy at birth. (2) Knowledge and education — adult literacy rate and combined gross enrolment ratio. (3) A decent standard of living — GDP per capita at purchasing power parity in US$. India is in the medium category near the bottom — 128 of 177 countries in 2007–08 — showing that high growth has not yet improved quality of life for all.

or: Explain the major efforts made for 'Education for All' in India.

(1) National Policy on Education 1986 — free and compulsory education up to 14. (2) 86th Amendment 2002 and RTE Act 2009 — education a Fundamental Right for 6–14. (3) Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan 2001 — enrolment, bridging gender and social gaps, retention, quality. (4) Mid-day Meal Scheme — nutrition and attendance. (5) National Literacy Mission 1988 — adult literacy through Total Literacy Campaign, Post Literacy and Continuing Education. (6) Results — primary schools within 1 km for 95% of rural people; literacy 52.21% (1991) to 65.37% (2001); more girls, SC and ST children enrolled.

la: Why are there regional imbalances and socio-economic disparities in India? Analyse any six factors.

(1) Colonial history — areas of no commercial interest were ignored. (2) Geography — deserts and difficult hilly terrain. (3) Unequal distribution and poor use of natural resources (Bihar, Jharkhand, Orissa). (4) Remoteness from national markets (North-East). (5) Lack of basic infrastructure — roads, electricity, transport — which discourages investment. (6) Poor governance and law-and-order problems, leading to under-use of allocated funds. These show up as differences in per capita income, poverty, industry, agriculture, literacy and roads.
